Inclusion probabilities and design weights

Source: R/inclusion.R
inclusion_prob.Rd

inclusion_prob() returns the first-order inclusion probability of every row of data under design — the probability that the row lands in a sample — without drawing one. sampling_weight() returns 1 / inclusion_prob(), the number of population units each sampled row stands for.

Usage

inclusion_prob(data, design, simulate = FALSE, R = 5000, seed = NULL)

sampling_weight(data, design, simulate = FALSE, R = 5000, seed = NULL)

Arguments

data

A data frame.

design

A design object.

simulate

Estimate the probabilities by repeated draws rather than in closed form. Required for the designs listed above; allowed for any probability design, which is a convenient way to check the exact formulas.

R

Number of simulated draws when simulate = TRUE. See "What a simulation costs".

seed

Optional seed for the simulation, applied as in draw() (see "Seeding" there). Checked whether or not simulate is TRUE.

Value

A numeric vector with one element per row of data.

A row the design can never select gets 0 from inclusion_prob() and NA from sampling_weight(), since no finite number of population rows is represented by a row that cannot be drawn. Such a row lies outside the region or the time window, comes past max_items, or was dropped under na_rm = TRUE. sample_summary() counts them. A weight of 0 is not one of these. The designs that select in proportion to size refuse it, so drop such rows from data first.

A design that draw() refuses, such as an n larger than the frame or than the rows inside a region, is refused here too, with the same message, rather than given probabilities above 1 or a census.

Details

These are what make a sample usable for estimation. A Horvitz-Thompson total is sum(y / pi) over the sampled rows, and its unbiasedness rests entirely on pi being the design's real inclusion probability rather than a plausible guess.

Which designs have a closed form

Most do, and those are computed exactly:

design_simple()n / N
design_stratified()n_h / N_h within each stratum
design_systematic()1 / interval with a random start, or n / N with n, for every row walked, exactly
design_cluster()n_clusters / N_clusters; with balanced = TRUE, that times the cluster's average take over its size, worked out exactly (see design_cluster())
design_multistage()(n_clusters / N_clusters) * (n_h / N_h), when the per-cluster take n_h is constant; with replacement, (n_clusters / N_clusters) * (1 - (1 - 1 / N_h)^n_h); with size, the cluster's pi_h = n_clusters * M_h / sum(M) in place of n_clusters / N_clusters
design_weighted()n * p_i for the "systematic" and "poisson" methods, with rows past 1 taken with certainty and the rest rescaled to sum to n; with strata, n_h * p_i within each stratum
design_certainty()1 above the threshold, rest's own below it
design_reservoir()n / min(N, max_items), and 0 past max_items
design_temporal()per_interval / N_bucket within each interval
design_spatial()n / N_in_region
design_spread()n / N, or n * p_i with a size column; with strata, the same within each stratum

A design with reserve gives the probabilities of its main sample, which the reserves do not change. The design of a sample from use_reserves() gives n / (N - u), and 0 for the u rows found unavailable.

Four cases have no closed form, and the package refuses to invent one:

  • design_multistage(allocation = "proportional") — the stage-two allocation depends on which clusters were selected. Simulation on clusters of 3/5/7/9 gives 0.17, 0.20, 0.17, 0.15, against a naive 0.33, 0.20, 0.14, 0.11.

  • design_multistage() where the per-cluster take is not constant — n not divisible by n_clusters, or, without replacement, a cluster smaller than n / n_clusters. The allocation runs over the selected clusters, so the remainder goes to the largest of them and an undersized cluster is capped with its shortfall dealt to whichever clusters came with it. A row's probability then depends on the company it keeps. On clusters of 20/10/8/6 with n = 7 over 2 clusters, the average take is out by up to 17%, and a cluster smaller than the take can push the figure above 1.

    For these two, the exact probability is the probability given the clusters selected, averaged over every possible selection, and that average has no formula. draw(weights = TRUE) weights the sample conditional on the clusters it selected instead, which gives an unbiased total without the average; see "Design weights" in draw().

  • design_weighted(method = "successive") — the default. Successive sampling has no closed-form inclusion probability; this is the whole reason the other two methods exist. Note that its realised probabilities are not merely unknown but genuinely different from proportional-to-size: for weights 1:10 at n = 5, enumerating every ordered draw puts them up to about 36% away.

  • design_bootstrap() — resampling with replacement from the sample is not a probability sample of a finite population, so there is no pi to report.

A design_systematic() with a fixed start is refused too, for another reason. It is deterministic: each row has probability 0 or 1, and simulate = TRUE reports exactly that. Without simulate those values are refused, because draw(weights = TRUE) would give every sampled row a weight of 1 and ht_total() would report the sum over the sample as the total of the frame. So are sampling_weight(), joint_prob(), draw(weights = TRUE) and the estimators. Leave start as NULL for a probability sample.

For all but the bootstrap, pass simulate = TRUE to estimate them by Monte Carlo instead. The estimate carries R-sized error, which is fine for checking a design and not fine for publishing a variance. Simulating a bootstrap is refused rather than answered: every row turns up in some replicate, so the count converges to 1 for all of them.

What a simulation costs

simulate = TRUE makes R draws, 5,000 by default, so it takes R times as long as one draw(). Most designs draw from a frame of 10,000 rows in well under a second. The local pivotal method of design_spread() does work in proportion to N^2 on every draw, so at 10,000 rows each draw takes seconds and the default R takes hours. When the draws after the first two, which carry one-off costs, project a run of more than 30 seconds, a message says how long it will take, and an interactive session shows a progress bar. Lower R for a quicker answer with more Monte Carlo error: its standard error is sqrt(p * (1 - p) / R), at most 0.007 for R = 5000.

A warning that every draw raises, such as a stratum allocated no rows or max_items cutting a frame short, is given once at the end, with the number of draws that raised it.

See also

draw(), which attaches these to a sample when weights = TRUE.

Examples

df <- data.frame(id = 1:20, site = rep(c("a", "b"), times = c(15, 5)))

# 8 rows allocated proportionally: 6 of 15, then 2 of 5
inclusion_prob(df, design_stratified("site", n = 8))
#>  [1] 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.4
#> [20] 0.4

sampling_weight(df, design_stratified("site", n = 8))
#>  [1] 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5
#> [20] 2.5

# The default weighted design has no closed form; ask for a simulation
w <- data.frame(id = 1:5, w = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 16))
inclusion_prob(w, design_weighted("w", n = 2), simulate = TRUE, R = 2000,
               seed = 1)
#> [1] 0.2785 0.2310 0.2700 0.2465 0.9740

# Systematic PPS does have one, and it is exactly proportional to size
inclusion_prob(w, design_weighted("w", n = 2, method = "systematic"))
#> [1] 0.25 0.25 0.25 0.25 1.00
